title: A First-Timer's History & Art Tour of Seoul: 2 Nights, 3 Days Itinerary
html:
Seoul has a surprising amount of history and art packed into a small area — royal palaces built over 600 years ago sit just a few subway stops from museums showing cutting-edge Korean contemporary art. If you like museums, old buildings, and beautiful things in general, this 2 nights, 3 days plan is built just for you. It mixes free palaces, free national museums, and a couple of paid stops that are worth every won.

Quick note before you start: almost every museum and palace on this list is closed one day a week (usually Monday or Tuesday), so check the "Before You Go" planning box near the end before you lock in your dates.

Day 1: Royal Palaces and Traditional Art (Jongno-gu)

Day 1 stays in one neighborhood, Jongno-gu (pronounced "jong-no-goo"), the old royal district of Seoul. Everything below is walkable from each other.

Gyeongbokgung Palace

Gyeongbokgung (pronounced "gyeong-bok-goong") is the biggest and most famous palace in Korea, first built in 1395. Giant wooden gates, painted roofs, and a throne hall called Geunjeongjeon make this the most "wow" photo spot on this whole trip. Admission is just 3,000 KRW (about $2), and the palace is closed every Tuesday. If you (or a friend) rent a hanbok (traditional Korean outfit, available from shops right outside the palace) and wear the full outfit, you get in completely free. Take the subway to Gyeongbokgung Station (Line 3), Exit 5.


Photo: Richard Mortel, via Wikimedia Commons (license per file page)

National Palace Museum of Korea & National Folk Museum (Both Free)

Right next to Gyeongbokgung's main entrance is the National Palace Museum of Korea — royal crowns, furniture, and documents from the Joseon Dynasty, all free to see. Inside the palace grounds (a short walk) is the National Folk Museum of Korea, which shows how regular Korean people actually lived and ate and dressed throughout history — a nice contrast to all the royal stuff. Both are free, and both are a good backup plan if it starts raining.


Photo via Wikimedia Commons (license per file page)

MMCA Seoul — Contemporary Art Inside a Historic Compound

A 10-minute walk from Gyeongbokgung is MMCA Seoul (National Museum of Modern and Contemporary Art, Seoul branch), built on the grounds of an old government building. This is where you go for contemporary Korean and international art — paintings, video art, installations, all in bright modern galleries mixed in with the preserved historic buildings. The permanent collection is free; some special exhibitions charge a fee. Here's a local secret: on Wednesday and Saturday evenings (6 PM–9 PM), admission to paid exhibitions is free too, which is exactly when a lot of Seoul locals come after work or on a date — so those evenings are busier but a great vibe if you don't mind the crowd.


Photo via Wikimedia Commons (license per file page)

Insadong — Traditional Art Street and Tea Houses

End Day 1 in Insadong (pronounced "in-sa-dong"), a neighborhood packed with small art galleries, antique shops, calligraphy stores, and traditional tea houses. It's less "big institution" and more "wander around and pop into tiny galleries," which is a nice change of pace after two museums. Many galleries here are free to browse. Get off at Anguk Station (Line 3), Exit 6.


Photo: Choi2451, CC BY-SA 3.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Day 2: National Treasures and World-Class Collections (Yongsan)

Day 2 moves to Yongsan (pronounced "yong-san"), home to the single biggest museum in Korea and one of the most talked-about private art museums in Asia.

National Museum of Korea

This is the National Museum of Korea, the largest museum in the country, covering thousands of years of Korean history in one enormous building. Give yourself at least 2–3 hours here — it's genuinely huge. The permanent exhibition is free, and it's a favorite rainy-day spot for Seoul locals for exactly that reason. Take the subway to Ichon Station (Line 4 or the Gyeongui-Jungang Line), Exit 2, and follow the signs — it's a short walk.


Photo: Ian Muttoo, CC BY-SA 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Leeum Museum of Art

Leeum Museum of Art (run by the Samsung Foundation) is one of Korea's most famous private museums, split between traditional Korean art and contemporary art, in buildings designed by three different world-famous architects. This one is not free — full access is around 20,000 KRW — and it's closed on Mondays. The important part: tickets must be booked online in advance (slots usually open about two weeks ahead), and they do sell out, especially on weekends. Don't show up without a ticket expecting to buy one at the door. Nearest station: Hangangjin Station (Line 6), Exit 1.


Photo: takato marui, via Wikimedia Commons (license per file page)

Day 3: A Small Palace and Seoul's Futuristic Side (Jung-gu & Dongdaemun)

Your last day pairs a smaller, quieter palace with two very different flavors of modern Seoul.

Deoksugung Palace and the Royal Guard Ceremony

Deoksugung (pronounced "duck-soo-goong") is smaller and calmer than Gyeongbokgung, with a pretty stone wall walkway that's especially nice in autumn. It's also the only palace in Seoul with a Western-style stone building inside it, left over from the early 1900s. Try to time your visit around the free Changing of the Royal Guard ceremony at the main gate, held at 11:00, 14:00, and 15:30. Admission is only 1,000 KRW, and it's closed on Mondays. Nearest station: City Hall Station (Line 1 or 2), Exit 2.


Photo via Wikimedia Commons (license per file page)

Seoul Museum of Art (SeMA)

Literally next door to Deoksugung is the Seoul Museum of Art (SeMA), the city's own contemporary art museum, housed in a building that mixes an old stone facade with a modern interior. Admission to the permanent collection is free (special exhibitions may charge), and like Deoksugung, it's closed on Mondays — easy to combine since they're a two-minute walk apart.


Photo: Ollie Palmer, CC BY-SA 4.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Dongdaemun Design Plaza (DDP)

Finish the trip somewhere completely different: Dongdaemun Design Plaza, usually just called DDP. Designed by architect Zaha Hadid, it's a huge, curvy, silver building with almost no straight lines — it looks like a spaceship landed in the middle of Seoul. Walking into the building itself and the rooftop park is free; design and art exhibitions inside have separate tickets. It's especially striking lit up at night, and the surrounding Dongdaemun area has 24-hour shopping and night markets if you want to keep going after dark. Exhibition halls are closed on Mondays. Nearest station: Dongdaemun History & Culture Park Station (Lines 2, 4, or 5), Exit 1.


Photo: Eugene Lim, CC BY 2.0, via Wikimedia Commons

Before You Go: Planning Around Closed Days

The one thing that can wreck this itinerary is showing up on the wrong day. Here's the pattern: Gyeongbokgung (Day 1) is closed Tuesdays, while Leeum, Deoksugung, SeMA, and DDP's exhibitions (Days 2–3) are all closed Mondays. In practice, that means: don't start this itinerary on a day where Day 1 would fall on a Tuesday, and don't let Day 2 or Day 3 land on a Monday. If your trip only allows for one of those days, just swap that day's order around — for example, do Day 3 first if your middle day is a Monday.

meta_description: A beginner-friendly 2-night, 3-day Seoul itinerary: royal palaces, the National Museum of Korea, Leeum, MMCA, and Insadong's art galleries, with hours and fees.
